result.party_text: The question is whether the father intended to gift the beneficial interest in the accounts to his daughter or intended her to hold the assets in trust for his estate.
result.why: The court states the question of the father's intent regarding beneficial interest in the accounts.

result.party_text: The appeal raises four issues: whether the presumptions of resulting trust and advancement continue to apply in modern times; the standard to rebut these presumptions; how courts should treat survivorship in joint accounts; and what evidence courts may consider to determine the transferor's intent.
result.why: The court explicitly lists the four issues raised on appeal.

result.party_text: The trial judge found that the father actually intended a gift and held that his daughter may retain the assets in the accounts.
result.why: The court notes the trial judge's finding that the father intended a gift and the daughter may retain the assets.

result.party_text: The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal of the daughter's ex-husband.
result.why: The court states the Court of Appeal dismissed the ex-husband's appeal.

result.party_text: The trial judge found the presumption of advancement applied given Paula's relationship with her father and that evidence failed to rebut it, so the money in the joint accounts belonged to Paula.
result.why: The court accepts the trial judge's finding that the presumption of advancement applied and was not rebutted, so the money belonged to Paula.

result.party_text: The trial judge found Paula's father intended to gift beneficial ownership of the assets to Paula while managing them before his death.
result.why: The court accepts the trial judge's finding that Paula's father intended to gift beneficial ownership to Paula.

result.why: The court accepts the Court of Appeal's agreement that there was ample evidence of the father's intention to give Paula beneficial interest.

result.party_text: The Court of Appeal found it unnecessary to rely on the presumption of advancement when there is evidence of actual intention.
result.why: The court accepts the Court of Appeal's finding that it was unnecessary to rely on the presumption of advancement when actual intention evidence exists.

result.party_text: While the trustee almost always has the legal title, in exceptional circumstances it is also possible that the trustee has equitable title.
result.why: The court accepts that while trustees usually have legal title, in exceptional cases they may have equitable title.

result.party_text: In the context of the parent-child relationship, the term advancement has also been used because the father was under a moral duty to advance his children in the world.
result.why: The court accepts that advancement is used in parent-child context because of the father's moral duty to advance his children.

result.party_text: Historically, the presumption of advancement applies where the transferor is a husband to his wife or a father to his child.
result.why: The court confirms the presumption applies where transferor is husband to wife or father to child.

result.party_text: Canadian courts are divided on whether the presumption of advancement applies between mother and child.
result.why: The court acknowledges Canadian courts are divided on presumption applying between mother and child.

result.party_text: Some courts have concluded the presumption of advancement should not apply between parents and adult independent children, due to modern social conditions and the common practice of adding adult children to accounts for assistance rather than as gifts.
result.why: The court agrees some courts reject presumption for adult independent children due to social conditions and joint accounts.

result.party_text: The independence and living situation of adult children are factors leading some courts to reject the presumption of advancement in transfers to adult children.
result.answer_quote: 36 I am inclined to agree. First, given that a principal justification for the presumption of advancement is parental obligation to support their dependent children, it seems to me that the presumption should not apply in respect of independent adult children. As Heeney J. noted in McLear, at para. 36, parental support obligations under provincial and federal statutes normally end when the child is no longer considered by law to be a minor: see e.g. Family Law Act, s. 31. Indeed, not only do child support obligations end when a child is no longer dependent, but often the reverse is true: an obligation may be imposed on independent adult children to support their parents in accordance with need and ability to pay: see e.g. Family Law Act, s. 32. Second, I agree with Heeney J. that it is common nowadays for ageing parents to transfer their assets into joint accounts with their adult children in order to have that child assist them in managing their financial affairs. There should therefore be a rebuttable presumption that the adult child is holding the property in trust for the ageing parent to facilitate the free and efficient management of that parent’s affairs.
result.why: The court agrees independence and living situation of adult children justify rejecting presumption of advancement.

result.party_text: Some commentators and courts argue that the presumption of advancement should apply to adult, independent children based on parental affection.
result.answer_quote: Indeed, the factor of affection applies in other relationships as well, such as between siblings, yet the presumption of advancement would not apply in those circumstances. However, I see no reason why courts cannot consider evidence relating to the quality of the relationship between the transferor and transferee in order to determine whether the presumption of a resulting trust has been rebutted.
result.why: The court rejects affection as basis for presumption applying to adult independent children.

result.party_text: The presumption of advancement should apply to adult dependent children.
result.answer_quote: 39 The question of whether the presumption applies to adult dependent children begs the question of what constitutes dependency for the purpose of applying the presumption. Dependency is a term susceptible to an enormous variety of circumstances. The extent or degree of dependency can be very wide ranging. While it may be rational to presume advancement as a result of dependency in some cases, in others it will not. For example, it is not difficult to accept that in some cases a parent would feel a moral, if not legal, obligation to provide for the quality of life for an adult disabled child. This might especially be the case where the disabled adult child is under the charge and care of the parent. 40 As compelling as some cases might be, I am reluctant to apply the presumption of advancement to gratuitous transfers to “dependent” adult children because it would be impossible to list the wide variety of the circumstances that make someone “dependent” for the purpose of applying the presumption. Courts would have to determine on a case-by-case basis whether or not a particular individual is “dependent”, creating uncertainty and unpredictability in almost every instance. I am therefore of the opinion that the rebuttable presumption of advancement with regard to gratuitous transfers from parent to child should be preserved but be limited in application to transfers by mothers and fathers to minor children.
result.why: The court rejects applying presumption to adult dependent children due to uncertainty and limits presumption to minors.

result.party_text: Dependency justifies presumption of advancement in some cases, such as for adult disabled children under parental care.
result.why: Court accepts that dependency can justify presumption of advancement in some cases, such as adult disabled children under parental care.

result.party_text: The party claiming that a transfer between a parent and an adult child is a gift can rebut the presumption of resulting trust by bringing evidence to support the claim.
result.why: Court accepts that the party claiming a transfer is a gift can rebut the presumption by bringing evidence.

result.party_text: Evidence as to the degree of dependency of an adult transferee child on the transferor parent may provide strong evidence to rebut the presumption of a resulting trust, even though dependency is not a basis to apply the presumption of advancement.
result.why: Court accepts that evidence of degree of dependency may rebut presumption of resulting trust, though dependency doesn't apply presumption of advancement.

result.party_text: Some cases suggest that the criminal standard or a higher than civil standard is required to rebut the presumption of resulting trust.
result.why: Court notes some cases suggest criminal or higher than civil standard to rebut presumption of resulting trust but later prefers civil standard.

result.party_text: Some cases suggest that only slight evidence is required to rebut the presumption of advancement.
result.why: Court accepts some cases suggest only slight evidence is required to rebut presumption of advancement.

result.party_text: Where the transferor intended to gift withdrawal rights and the balance on death through survivorship, courts find the presumption of resulting trust rebutted and the transferee entitled to the balance on death.
result.why: Court accepts that where transferor intended to gift withdrawal rights and balance on death, presumption of resulting trust is rebutted.

result.party_text: In some cases, transferors place assets in joint accounts intending to retain exclusive control until death, with the transferee taking the balance through survivorship.
result.why: The court accepts that transferors may place assets in joint accounts intending to retain control until death with survivorship to transferee.

result.party_text: Transferors may place assets in joint accounts to get assistance managing finances, avoid probate fees, and simplify after-death disposition.
result.why: The court accepts that transferors may place assets in joint accounts for assistance managing finances, avoiding probate fees, and simplifying after-death disposition.

result.party_text: Courts have struggled whether to give effect to transferor's intention when beneficial interest arises only on death, with some judges treating survivorship gifts as testamentary and invalid if not in proper form.
result.answer_quote: For the reasons that follow, however, I am of the view that the rights of survivorship, both legal and equitable, vest when the joint account is opened and the gift of those rights is therefore inter vivos in nature. This has also been the conclusion of the weight of judicial opinion in recent times: see e.g. Mordo v. Nitting, [2006] B.C.J. No. 3081 (QL), 2006 BCSC 1761, at paras. 233-38; Shaw v. MacKenzie Estate (1994), 4 E.T.R. (2d) 306 (N.S.S.C.), at para. 49; and Reber v. Reber (1988), 48 D.L.R. (4th) 376 (B.C.S.C.); see also Waters’ Law of Trusts, at p. 406. 49 An early case that addressed the issue of the nature of survivorship is Re Reid in which Ferguson J.A. of the Ontario Court of Appeal found that the gift of a joint interest was a “complete and perfect gift inter vivos” (p. 608) from the moment that the joint account was opened even though the transferor in that case retained exclusive control over the account during his lifetime. I agree with this interpretation. I also find MacKay J.A.’s reasons in Edwards v. Bradley (C.A.), at p. 234, to be persuasive: The legal right to take the balance in the account if A predeceases him being vested in B on the opening of the account, it cannot be the subject of a testamentary disposition. If A’s intention was that B should also have the beneficial interest, B already has the legal title and there is nothing further to be done to complete the gift of the beneficial interest. If A’s intention was that B should not take the beneficial interest, it belongs to A or his estate and he is not attempting to dispose of it by means of the joint account. In either event B has the legal title and the only question that can arise on A’s death is whether B is entitled to keep any money that may be in the account on A’s death or whether he holds it as a trustee under a resulting trust for A’s estate. [Emphasis added.] Edwards v. Bradley was appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada but the issue of survivorship was not addressed.
result.why: The court acknowledges courts have struggled but ultimately holds survivorship rights vest inter vivos, rejecting the view that survivorship gifts are testamentary and invalid.

result.party_text: Some judges argue that a gift of survivorship cannot be a complete and perfect inter vivos gift because the transferor can drain the joint account before death.
result.answer_quote: The nature of a joint account is that the balance will fluctuate over time. The gift in these circumstances is the transferee’s survivorship interest in the account balance — whatever it may be — at the time of the transferor’s death, not to any particular amount.
result.why: The court rejects the argument that survivorship gifts cannot be complete inter vivos gifts due to transferor's ability to drain the account before death.

result.party_text: Some courts have departed from the restrictive rule in Shephard v. Cartwright regarding admissibility of subsequent evidence.
result.why: The court acknowledges some courts have departed from the restrictive rule in Shephard v. Cartwright.

result.party_text: In Neazor v. Hoyle, the trial judge considered conduct of parties years after transfer to determine beneficial ownership.
result.why: The court cites Neazor v. Hoyle where conduct after transfer was considered to determine beneficial ownership.

result.party_text: The rule excluding subsequent evidence has lost much of its force in England.
result.why: The court states the rule excluding subsequent evidence has lost much of its force in England.

result.party_text: The Court of Appeal held that control of the account was not determinative of Paula's father's intentions regarding beneficial interest.
result.why: The Court of Appeal held control was not determinative of the father's intentions regarding beneficial interest.

result.party_text: In Madsen Estate, the Court of Appeal found that the father's retention of control and payment of taxes indicated no intention to create a beneficial joint tenancy.
result.why: The Court of Appeal in Madsen Estate found father's control and tax payment indicated no intention to create beneficial joint tenancy.

result.party_text: In Madsen Estate, the Court of Appeal did not view granting power of attorney as negating the joint account as a tool of convenience.
result.why: The court notes Madsen Estate did not view power of attorney as negating joint account as a convenience tool.

result.party_text: The Court of Appeal in the present case placed substantial weight on the transferor granting joint ownership and power of attorney as evidence of intent to gift assets.
result.why: The court acknowledges the Court of Appeal placed substantial weight on joint ownership and power of attorney as evidence of intent to gift.

result.party_text: Lang J.A. reasoned that power of attorney alone would suffice for managing accounts, so joint ownership indicated intent to gift and avoid probate fees.
result.why: The court records Lang J.A.'s reasoning that power of attorney alone suffices for managing accounts, so joint ownership indicates intent to gift.

result.party_text: Lang J.A. found that the weight of evidence is a matter within the trial judge's discretion.
result.why: The court agrees that the weight of evidence is within the trial judge's discretion.

result.party_text: Courts have relied to varying degrees on the transferor’s tax treatment of the account in determining intent.
result.why: The court confirms courts have relied on transferor's tax treatment in determining intent.

result.party_text: In Madsen Estate, the trial judge relied in part on the fact that the transferor was the one who declared and paid income tax on the money in the joint accounts in finding that the transferor intended a resulting trust.
result.why: The court notes in Madsen Estate the trial judge relied on transferor paying income tax as evidence of intent for resulting trust.

result.party_text: In the present case, the trial judge noted that Paula’s father continued to pay taxes on the income in joint accounts but nevertheless found that he intended to gift the joint accounts to her.
result.answer_quote: I do not find either of these approaches inappropriate. The weight to be placed on tax-related evidence in determining a transferor’s intent should be left to the discretion of the trial judge. However, whether or not a transferor continues to pay taxes on the income earned in the joint accounts during his or her lifetime should not be determinative of his or her intention in the absence of other evidence. For example, it may be that the transferor made the transfer for the sole purpose of obtaining assistance in the management of his or her finances and wished to have the assets form a part of his or her estate upon his or her death. Or, as discussed above, it is open to a transferor to gift the right of survivorship to the transferee when the joint accounts are opened, but to retain control over the use of the funds in the accounts (and therefore to continue to pay taxes on them) during his or her lifetime.
result.why: The court accepts the trial judge's finding that the father intended to gift the accounts despite paying taxes on income.

result.party_text: For public policy reasons, transferors should not be permitted to transfer beneficial title while asserting to tax authorities that such title has not been passed to defer or avoid taxes on capital gains.
result.answer_quote: In principle, I agree. Where, in setting up a joint account, the transferor intends to transfer full legal and equitable title to the assets in the account immediately and the value of the assets reflects a capital gain, taxes on capital gains may become payable in the year the joint account is set up. However, where the transferor’s intention is to gift the right of survivorship to the transferee but retain beneficial ownership of the assets during his or her lifetime, there would appear to be no disposition at the moment of the setting up of the joint account: see s. 73 of the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp .). That said, the issue of the proper treatment of capital gains in the setting up of joint accounts was not argued in this appeal. I can say no more than these are matters for determination between the Canada Revenue Agency and taxpayers in specific cases.
result.why: The court agrees in principle with the public policy concern but notes the issue was not argued and leaves it to tax authorities.

result.party_text: The trial judge found Paula and her father had a very close relationship and that Paula was the person he was closest to besides his wife.
result.why: The court accepts the trial judge's finding of a very close relationship between Paula and her father.

result.party_text: Given Paula's financial hardships, her father preferred her over her siblings.
result.why: The court accepts the finding that the father preferred Paula over her siblings due to her financial hardships.

result.party_text: The father was estranged from one daughter when the accounts were set up.
result.why: The court accepts the finding that the father was estranged from one daughter when the accounts were set up.

result.party_text: The father was close to his son-in-law but they were only good friends.
result.why: The court accepts the finding that the father was close to his son-in-law but only good friends.

result.why: The court agrees the wife was seriously ill and not expected to outlive the father.

result.why: The court accepts that Paula and her family relied on her father financially.

result.party_text: The father maintained control of the accounts and used the funds for his benefit during his life but intended to provide for Paula after his death.
result.why: The court accepts the father controlled the accounts but intended to provide for Paula after death.

result.party_text: This is consistent with an intention to gift a right of survivorship when the accounts were set up.
result.why: The court agrees this is consistent with gifting a right of survivorship.

result.party_text: Statements of Paula’s father while drafting his last will indicate his intention regarding the accounts.
result.answer_quote: This evidence indicates that Paula’s father was of the view that the accounts had already been dealt with and understood these assets would not form part of the estate. I agree with the trial judge that “if [the father’s] intention was to have his jointly held assets devolve through the estate, they were of such magnitude that he would have at least discussed that matter with his solicitor, since they constituted a substantial proportion of what he owned” (para. 43), particularly after the lawyer asked him about life insurance policies, RRIFs and other assets. All of this evidence is consistent with Paula’s father having gifted away the right of survivorship when the joint accounts were opened, and thus is relevant to his intention at the time of the transfer.
result.why: The court accepts the statements indicate the father's intention about the accounts.

result.party_text: The trial judge considered the lawyer’s testimony about the father’s statements reliable as the lawyer had nothing to gain.
result.why: The court accepts the lawyer's testimony was reliable and unbiased.

result.party_text: The evidence indicates the father viewed the accounts as already dealt with and not part of the estate.
result.answer_quote: I agree with the trial judge that “if [the father’s] intention was to have his jointly held assets devolve through the estate, they were of such magnitude that he would have at least discussed that matter with his solicitor, since they constituted a substantial proportion of what he owned” (para. 43), particularly after the lawyer asked him about life insurance policies, RRIFs and other assets. All of this evidence is consistent with Paula’s father having gifted away the right of survivorship when the joint accounts were opened, and thus is relevant to his intention at the time of the transfer.
result.why: The court agrees the evidence shows the father viewed the accounts as already dealt with and not part of the estate.

result.party_text: The father wrote letters to financial institutions stating the transfers were not gifts to Paula.
result.answer_quote: The trial judge found that Paula’s father’s intention when he wrote the letters was “simply to avoid triggering an immediate deemed disposition of the assets in question, and therefore avoid capital gains taxes” (para. 39). I agree with the trial judge that this is not inconsistent with an intention that the balance remaining in the accounts would belong to Paula on his death.
result.why: The court accepts the father wrote letters but finds his intention was to avoid immediate tax, not to deny gift intention.

result.party_text: The father continued to control the funds and paid income tax on earnings before his death.
result.answer_quote: The trial judge found that Paula’s father’s intention when he wrote the letters was “simply to avoid triggering an immediate deemed disposition of the assets in question, and therefore avoid capital gains taxes” (para. 39). I agree with the trial judge that this is not inconsistent with an intention that the balance remaining in the accounts would belong to Paula on his death.
result.why: The court accepts the father controlled funds and paid taxes, consistent with his intention to avoid immediate tax consequences.

result.party_text: The trial judge found the father’s intention in writing the letters was to avoid triggering immediate deemed disposition and capital gains taxes.
result.answer_quote: I agree with the trial judge that this is not inconsistent with an intention that the balance remaining in the accounts would belong to Paula on his death.
result.why: The court agrees the trial judge correctly found the father's intention was to avoid immediate tax consequences.

result.party_text: The trial judge erred in applying the presumption of advancement because Paula was not a minor child.
result.answer_quote: Nonetheless, this error does not affect the ultimate disposition of the appeal because the trial judge found that the evidence “clearly demonstrate[d] the intention” on the part of the father that the balance left in the joint accounts he had with Paula were to go to Paula alone on his death through survivorship (para. 44). I am satisfied that this strong finding regarding the father’s actual intention shows that the trial judge’s conclusion would have been the same even if he had applied the presumption of a resulting trust.
result.why: The court agrees the trial judge erred in applying the presumption but finds the error did not affect the outcome.

result.party_text: Michael Pecore asked this Court for costs throughout from Paula or the estate.
result.answer_quote: As noted in the judgment of the Ontario Court of Appeal, at para. 48, the trial judge denied Michael costs out of the estate or from Paula. He did so because he found that on the issues raised in the divorce proceeding, success was divided, Paula made an offer to settle that exceeded the result, and Michael’s conduct was “less than candid”. I see no reason to interfere with that disposition, or that costs should not follow the event in this Court.
result.why: The court rejects the request for costs, upholding the trial judge's denial due to divided success and Michael's conduct.

result.party_text: The trial judge denied Michael costs out of the estate or from Paula because success was divided, Paula made an offer to settle that exceeded the result, and Michael’s conduct was less than candid.
result.answer_quote: I see no reason to interfere with that disposition, or that costs should not follow the event in this Court.
result.why: The court affirms the trial judge's denial of costs for the stated reasons and sees no reason to interfere.

result.party_text: The trial judge applied the presumption of advancement and concluded the father intended to gift the money to his daughter, a decision upheld by the Court of Appeal.
result.why: The text confirms the trial judge applied the presumption of advancement and was upheld by the Court of Appeal.

result.party_text: The issue in the appeal is which presumption applies—the presumption of advancement or the presumption of resulting trust—and the consequences of its application.
result.why: The text explicitly states this is the issue in the appeal.

result.party_text: There is ongoing debate about whether the presumptions, especially the presumption of resulting trust, should be removed from judicial consideration because modern life makes the presumption of gift more plausible than the presumption of resulting trust.
result.why: The court acknowledges and discusses the ongoing debate and the criticisms of the presumption of resulting trust in modern context.

result.party_text: The traditional presumption of advancement as between husband and wife has been largely abandoned both judicially and legislatively.
result.why: The court confirms the presumption of advancement between husband and wife has been largely abandoned judicially and legislatively.

result.party_text: The presumption of advancement retains much of its original vigour in the case of gratuitous transfers to children.
result.why: The court accepts that the presumption retains much of its original vigour in gratuitous transfers to children.

result.party_text: Rothstein J. rejects parental affection as a basis for the presumption, stating the principal justification is parental obligation to support dependent children.
result.why: The court rejects Rothstein J.'s narrow view, affirming parental affection as a basis for the presumption alongside parental obligation.

result.party_text: The presumption of advancement between father and child has not been subjected to the same re-evaluation as between husband and wife because parental affection continues to exist and cannot be presumed in relationships between strangers.
result.why: The court accepts that the presumption between father and child remains due to parental affection, unlike between strangers.

result.party_text: Professor Freedman acknowledges the original rationale of the advancement rule is difficult to pin down and did not arise only from parental obligation to support dependent children.
result.why: The court accepts Professor Freedman's view that the original rationale is complex and not solely parental obligation.

result.party_text: Cullity J. observed parental affection grounds the presumption and is the greatest indicator of the probable intent of the transferor.
result.why: The court accepts Cullity J.'s observation that parental affection grounds the presumption and indicates transferor intent.

result.party_text: Because parental affection has historically been seen as a basis for the presumption of advancement, it was routinely applied to adult as well as minor children.
result.why: The court confirms the presumption was routinely applied to adult children based on parental affection.

result.party_text: Some courts in the mid-90s began questioning whether the presumption of advancement should apply to transfers between parents and their adult children.
result.why: The court acknowledges some courts questioned the presumption's application to adult children in the mid-90s.

result.party_text: The Ontario Court of Appeal accepted the trial judge's application of the presumption of advancement to a transfer by a father to his adult daughter.
result.why: The court notes the Ontario Court of Appeal accepted the presumption's application to an adult daughter.

result.party_text: The presumption of advancement in gratuitous transfers to children is not solely based on financial dependency but also on natural affection.
result.why: The court agrees the presumption is based on both financial dependency and natural affection.

result.party_text: It is flawed to argue that the presumption of advancement should not apply to adult children because elderly parents need assistance managing their finances.

result.party_text: The possibility of undue influence by adult children does not justify disregarding the presumption of advancement in most parent-child transfers.

result.why: The court accepts that the presumption of advancement applies to all gratuitous transfers from parents to children regardless of age or dependency.

result.party_text: The presumption of advancement is unique to the parental relationship due to its legal obligations and protective emotional ties, not just affection alone.
result.why: The court accepts that the presumption is unique to the parental relationship due to legal obligations and protective emotional ties, not just affection.

result.why: The court accepts that bank account documents confirming survivorship interest should be considered evidence of intention.
